title: WNBA faces eligibility test after Cunningham's transgender comments spark political attention
dek: Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said it was 'common sense' to bar transgender athletes from women's sports, drawing support from President Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom then declared himself a WNBA prospect, citing ambiguity in the league's eligibility rules. The WNBA has not publicly addressed the controversy.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The WNBA's collective bargaining agreement states 'Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA,' but the league has never had to define or defend what 'women' means under that language.
bottom_line: The WNBA will likely clarify its eligibility standards after Engelbert's meeting with team presidents, but the league has moved carefully rather than issuing an immediate ruling. Watch whether the league's formal policy addresses transgender women explicitly or reaffirms the existing CBA language without further definition. If the league issues a detailed policy, it would signal that ambiguity did exist; if it simply restates the current rule, it may suggest former players are testing the league's resolve rather than exploiting a genuine gap.
body: The WNBA confronts an immediate test of its eligibility framework after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham's high-profile comments on transgender athletes drew national political support and prompted former NBA players to signal they would exploit what they characterize as a loophole in the league's rules.

Cunningham, in her eighth WNBA season at age 29, said in an ESPN interview that she wanted to protect young girls "who shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sport. She later doubled down, saying it was "common sense" to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports, according to BBC Sport's reporting. President Donald Trump expressed support for her comments, and Vice President JD Vance called Cunningham "inspiring."

In response, Enes Kanter Freedom, who played 11 NBA seasons, declared on social media: "I'm officially declaring myself a WNBA prospect," per BBC Sport. His move was framed as a test of the league's eligibility language. The WNBA's collective bargaining agreement, negotiated between the league and its players association, states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." That language does not explicitly define what "women" means or address transgender status, according to the brief.

Cunningham later stated she is "not a very political person." She also denied her comments meant she "hated" transgender people, saying she wanted to "extend love" to everyone. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organized at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests.

No openly transgender woman is currently due to play in the WNBA, nor has one ever played in the league, according to BBC Sport. Despite the practical absence of the issue, the debate has drawn significant media and political attention.

League Commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week indicating the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents. In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league." The WNBA has not commented publicly on the controversy since Cunningham's initial remarks.

The row exposes an open question: whether the current eligibility language contains what former players view as a loophole, or whether the league's existing rule is clear and Kanter's declaration is a political gesture. What counts as "women" under the CBA and how the league defines that term remains unspecified in publicly available league statements.
